query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 0.5–1 at.% of yttrium (Y) during casting of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of a Y-enriched, thin, adherent oxide scale that significantly reduces oxygen ingress at high temperature without altering the alloy’s intrinsic mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated, as‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxidation resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor addition of approximately 0.5–1 at.% yttrium (Y) to the melt during the casting process.
generation.conditions: Exposure at around 1000 °C in an oxygen-containing (oxidizing) atmosphere for tens to hundreds of hours, with subsequent mechanical testing at room temperature and at 1000 °C under tensile loading at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of a Y-enriched, thin, adherent oxide scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Reactive element effect: the yttrium addition modifies the oxidation process so that a protective oxide layer forms with enhanced adhesion and slower growth kinetics, thereby inhibiting deep oxygen diffusion into the bulk without altering the internal microstructure responsible for ductility and high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Y-doped HfNbTaTiZr alloy will show a significantly reduced oxidation rate (evidenced by lower weight gain and thinner, more adherent oxide scales) when exposed at 1000 °C compared to the untreated alloy, while maintaining the original mechanical performance (8–16% RT ductility and yield strength within 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.baseline: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with acceptable mechanical performance but poor oxygen resistance.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable to alloys produced by casting that yield the conventional microstructure; the predicted benefits are expected under oxidizing conditions at around 1000 °C and under tensile strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹. Extreme exposure durations or deviations in processing that might alter microstructure are outside the bounds of this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide scale formation and its long-term stability over very extended exposure times remain uncertain, as does the potential for slight microstructural segregation influenced by Y addition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples using identical processing conditions: one set with a 0.5–1 at.% Y addition and one set without. Expose both sets to an oxygen-rich atmosphere at 1000 °C for 100 hours. After exposure, perform detailed oxidation characterization (using weight gain measurements and microscopy to assess oxide scale thickness and adherence) and conduct tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C (under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
measurements: Oxidation rate (oxide scale thickness and weight gain per unit area)
Oxide scale integrity (adherence and morphology via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate (i.e., similar oxide scale thickness and weight gain as untreated samples) OR if the mechanical properties deviate from the baseline ranges (room-temperature ductility below 8% or yield strength at 1000 °C falling outside 163–530 MPa), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

frame.system: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in its untreated, as‐cast state
frame.goal: Improve high-temperature oxygen resistance while preserving the alloy’s room‐temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength
frame.limitation: Poor oxygen resistance that limits its practical use at high temperature
constraints: No sacrifice of the alloy’s mechanical performance (8–16% RT ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C)
Must operate across strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹

regime.exposure_time: Realistic service durations (e.g., tens to hundreds of hours to simulate high-temperature exposure)
regime.mechanical_loading: Tensile loading at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹

prior_attempts: The baseline untreated cast alloy demonstrates acceptable mechanical properties but fails in oxygen resistance, implying that prior common approaches (e.g., conventional alloying or coatings) might have compromised the balance between oxidation protection and mechanical performance, though explicit attempts are not detailed in the question.
frame.understanding: It is hypothesized that a small addition (≈0.5–1 at.%) of a reactive element (e.g., yttrium, Y) introduced during casting could promote the in situ formation of a thin, adherent, and slow-growing protective oxide scale (via the reactive element effect). This scale would inhibit deep oxygen ingress without altering the bulk microstructure responsible for the ductility and high-temperature strength. The hypothesis predicts that Y-doped HfNbTaTiZr will maintain the unchanged mechanical performance in the as-cast state while exhibiting significantly improved oxidation resistance when exposed at 1000 °C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere for extended periods. A controlled falsification experiment would involve preparing two sets of samples under identical casting conditions – one set with the Y addition and one without – followed by high-temperature oxidation tests and mechanical testing (tensile tests conducted at room temperature and 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) to compare oxidation depth, scale adherence, ductility, and yield strength. If the Y-modified alloy fails to show a reduced oxidation rate or exhibits degraded mechanical properties compared to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis would be rejected.

decision.trend: Early work on refractory high‐entropy alloys has largely focused on preserving the desirable combination of room‐temperature ductility and high‐temperature strength through careful selection of processing routes (e.g., casting, HIP, directional solidification) and minor compositional adjustments (such as small additions of Cr or Hf, which modify phase formation and lattice parameters). These studies have succeeded in enhancing mechanical performance, but they have not specifically addressed high‐temperature oxygen resistance. In similar systems, adding minor reactive elements has been shown in related literature (for example, in Ni-based superalloys) to form thin, adherent oxide scales—a mechanism that has not yet been applied to this particular alloy composition.
decision.unsolved: While the as‐cast alloy meets the mechanical criteria (8–16% RT ductility and ∼163–530 MPa yield at 1000 °C), its poor oxygen resistance remains an open problem. No single-step intervention to promote a protective oxidation behavior without altering the bulk microstructure has been demonstrated in this alloy system.
decision.lever: introduce a minor addition (approximately 0.5–1 at.%) of a reactive element such as yttrium (Y) during casting
decision.why: This approach leverages the well‐documented reactive element effect, where small additions of Y are known to promote the in situ formation of a thin, adherent, and slow-growing oxide scale that can inhibit oxygen ingress. It builds directly on the trend of using subtle compositional modifications to finely tune phase formation without sacrificing mechanical performance, and it targets the specific limitation of oxygen resistance at 1000 °C in oxidizing environments.
